claims.visible_claim: This page uses a 30-facet NEO/IPIP-NEO interpretive framework. The official IPIP resource lists three sets of scales intended to measure constructs similar to the 30 NEO facets and distinguishes the historical and measurement traditions behind the lexical Big Five, FFM, BFI, and NEO/IPIP families ([S11](https://ipip.ori.org/Finding_Scales_to_Measure_Particular_Constructs.htm)). Other research has proposed different hierarchical arrangements, including a 10-aspect level ([S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17983306/)). Thirty facets are therefore not the one universal structure used by every Big Five instrument.
claims.boundary: Supports this package's labeled interpretive framework, not a universal facet hierarchy, scale equivalence, or product validity.
claims.source_section: The Facet Framework Used by FermatMind
claims.scientific_narrowing_reason: The English claim explicitly distinguishes this package's 30-facet NEO/IPIP-NEO vocabulary from alternative Big Five hierarchies and avoids implying a universal facet structure or scale equivalence.

claims.visible_claim: This content package uses the 30-facet vocabulary associated with the NEO and IPIP-NEO tradition. The NEO-PI-R manual describes six facets under each domain. The official IPIP resource provides public-item scales intended to measure constructs similar to those facets; it does not claim that those scales are identical to a proprietary instrument ([S11](https://ipip.ori.org/Finding_Scales_to_Measure_Particular_Constructs.htm)).
claims.boundary: Different Big Five instruments and scoring systems must not be treated as interchangeable.
claims.source_section: History and Limits of the 30-Facet Framework
claims.scientific_narrowing_reason: The English claim clarifies that public IPIP scales measure similar constructs and are not identical to a proprietary instrument, preventing scale-equivalence and product-validity inferences.
